questions.q: The six dispute replies are best used as:
o: Ignored — immaterial
Evidence on valuation/cutoff AND a population to test individually: returns in transit hit both revenue and inventory — evaluate each for the period it belongs
Reclassified automatically
Sent to legal
questions.why: Exceptions are diagnostic: returns-in-transit disputes at year-end straddle the cut-off; each needs its own treatment test (right of return provisions, revenue reversal timing), and the pattern across six is an audit-relevant trend, not noise.

questions.stem: Audit of Truline Distributors (wholesale, Rs 8,000 lakh receivables, 460 customers). The auditor sent 35 positive confirmations: 22 replied matching, 6 replied with disputes (returns in transit), 7 didn't reply. The client refuses more confirmations 'to protect customers'; also 9 large invoices were billed 31 March for goods that left 3 April.

questions.q: For the 7 non-replies:
o: Assume agreement
Perform alternative procedures (subsequent cash, shipping docs, order terms); where absent, treat the balance as unevidenced and project the effect into the misstatement evaluation
Ask the client to phone them
Confirm with a different 7
questions.why: A positive request without a response requires alternative evidence; no alternative evidence ⇒ that balance joins the 'unable to obtain evidence' pool — its size drives whether the gap is trivial, material, or pervasive.

questions.q: The client's refusal to allow more confirmations is:
o: Fine — 35 were sent
A management-imposed limitation to evaluate: why refuse? Consider fraud risk, the effect on evidence, opinion implications if material and pervasive
Accepted with a representation
Overruled by the audit firm
questions.why: Management restrictions on the audit scope are evaluated as a limitation (discuss, evaluate evidence sufficiency, implications for the opinion) — and the motive is itself risk information; SA 505/500 treat refusal like the representation refusal: evidence you can't get is a problem with consequences.

questions.q: The nine 31-March invoices for goods that left 3 April:
o: Leave — invoiced is recorded
Reverse revenue and re-add inventory (goods not shipped/title not passed by 31 March: revenue recognition criteria fail); adjust the cut-off and consider whether the pattern is intentional
Move to next year with a note
Ask the customers
questions.why: Bill-and-ship split across year-end = premature revenue: the performance obligation (transfer of control) occurs on 3 April — this year's revenue is overstated with the matching inventory; a repeated pattern in the last week hints at manipulation and changes the risk assessment too.

questions.q: If after all this the auditor's uncorrected AR misstatement totals Rs 190 lakh vs overall materiality Rs 150 lakh:
o: Ignore below PM
Aggregate with other uncorrected items, evaluate against materiality and qualitatively — likely material; decide qualified vs adverse by pervasiveness
Auto-withdraw
Disclose in KAM and sign
questions.why: SA 450: the sum of known + uncorrected judged against OM (and PM), then pervasiveness for the type; AR is a primary caption so material-and-pervasive is live — the answer is the modification matrix, not a preference.

questions.q: Which evidence is generally the MOST reliable under SA 500?
o: Oral management explanation
A photocopied invoice
Bank confirmation obtained directly by the auditor
A system-generated report from an IT environment with untested controls
questions.why: Reliability hierarchy: from independent external sources (direct confirmation) > original documents > evidence under controls operating effectively — copies and internal system reports rank below; oral explanations are the weakest written nowhere.
questions.trend: Repeated theme in recent ICAI exam question-patterns for this paper (AI pattern estimate — not a citation to a specific past paper question).
questions.probWhy: HIGH likelihood for Nov 2026 — auditor-gathered + independent + original = the gold triangle Prediction is study guidance, not an ICAI statement.

mem.tip: Evidence you fetch beats evidence you're fed.

questions.q: Under SA 505, the auditor:
o: Must confirm the entire ledger
Presumes accounts receivable confirmations are relevant for balances and rights claims, and evaluates refusal to allow confirmation as affecting opinion
Uses only negative confirmations
Sends requests through client staff with no restrictions
questions.why: SA 505 has a presumption for receivables confirmations; the response's reliability is higher when the auditor controls send/receive; management refusal = limitation to discuss, consider implications for fraud risk and opinion.
questions.trend: Core concept that appears in some avatar in most attempts under the new scheme (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — confirmation = auditor-controlled postage, or it isn't evidence AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: Letters through the client's hands are souvenirs.

questions.q: Negative confirmation requests provide LESS evidence because:
o: They are illegal
Non-response may mean agreement, oversight, or misdelivery — silence is not reply
They test only existence
They must be sent by courier
questions.why: Negative forms ask the debtor to respond only if disagreeing — silence is ambiguous; usable for large populations of small balances with low assessed risk, but never adequate ALONE (SA 505 says this in terms).
questions.trend: Known trap zone: ICAI objective papers repeatedly test limits/exceptions of this rule (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — silence is not assent in either direction in court AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: A quiet mailbox is not a signed statement.

questions.q: Analytical procedures are mandatory in:
o: Only substantive testing
The planning (risk identification) stage and the overall review at completion
Neither — they are optional
Only internal audit
questions.why: SA 520: analytics are REQUIRED as risk assessment procedures, REQUIRED as an overall review near completion, and OPTIONAL as substantive tests (where they can be powerfully efficient for predictable relationships).
questions.trend: Repeated theme in recent ICAI exam question-patterns for this paper (AI pattern estimate — not a citation to a specific past paper question).
questions.probWhy: HIGH likelihood for Nov 2026 — mandatory at both ends, optional in the middle Prediction is study guidance, not an ICAI statement.

mem.tip: Analytics bookend the audit: read the forecast, sign off on the story.

questions.q: A substantive analytical procedure's precision is undermined by:
o: A disaggregated expectation
Unreliable underlying data (e.g. unvalidated inventory quantities)
Expectations built from budgets vs actuals where budgets are tight
Using three years of history
questions.why: Precision depends on the quality of data used to build the expectation and the comparability/accuracy of the disaggregation; unreliable inputs cap the test's strength regardless of methodology — corroborating data reliability is part of the procedure.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — garbage in, elegant regression out Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

mem.ti: TI: Data reliability in substantive analytics
mem.tip: Your model is only as honest as its rawest input.

questions.q: In a test of controls, the tolerable deviation rate is 4%, expected population deviation rate 1.5%, and the computed upper deviation limit is 5.1%. The auditor should:
o: Accept controls — sample results support risk at the assessed level
Conclude the controls cannot be relied upon at the planned level (extend or go substantive)
Reduce tolerable rate
Report fraud
questions.why: Decision rule: compare the upper deviation limit (not the sample rate) to the TOLERABLE rate — 5.1 > 4.0 ⇒ risk of over-reliance is too high; revise assessed control risk downward-reliance, or extend testing, or switch to substantive.
questions.trend: Known trap zone: ICAI objective papers repeatedly test limits/exceptions of this rule (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — UDL vs tolerable rate — the one comparison that decides everything AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: Judge the worst plausible number, not the pretty average.

questions.q: Auditors stratify a population primarily when:
o: The population has large variability — to reduce each stratum's variation and sample size
The client prefers it
Every item is high-value
The tolerable rate is zero
questions.why: Stratification splits a variable population into sub-populations of similar items; with small within-stratum variation, a smaller total sample achieves the same precision — and high-value items may become 100% strata.
questions.trend: Core concept that appears in some avatar in most attempts under the new scheme (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — same dollars, fewer surprises — or more focus Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

mem.tip: Cut the deck by suits and you need fewer cards.

questions.q: An auditor applies the right test to the wrong population. This is:
o: Sampling risk
Non-sampling risk (human error in design/execution)
Tolerable deviation
Population error
questions.why: Sampling risk = wrong conclusion from testing less than 100% when the chosen procedure is sound; NON-sampling risk = everything else the auditor got wrong — wrong procedures, misreading an exception, wrong population — reducible by QA, not sample size.
questions.trend: Known trap zone: ICAI objective papers repeatedly test limits/exceptions of this rule (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — sampling risk shrinks with size; non-sampling with care AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: Bigger samples don't fix the wrong test.

questions.q: Confirmations are ideally dated:
o: A month after the year-end
At or near the balance-sheet date (earlier only with strong controls and roll-forward procedures)
At the AGM
Before the audit starts
questions.why: The date ties evidence to the reporting date; interim confirmations need control reliance + roll-forward to close the gap.
questions.trend: Core concept that appears in some avatar in most attempts under the new scheme (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — the closer to the 31st, the cleaner the evidence Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

mem.tip: Postcards need addresses that match the date stamp.

questions.q: Written representations are dated:
o: At the audit start
As near as practicable to, and not after, the date of the auditor's report
One year later
Before the FS approval
questions.why: Representations must cover the same period as the report — a stale-dated letter is a hole through the reporting window.
questions.trend: Known trap zone: ICAI objective papers repeatedly test limits/exceptions of this rule (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — date it last, cover it full Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

mem.tip: Signatures expire; the period must not.

questions.q: In attribute sampling the auditor measures:
o: Rupee errors
Rate of control DEVIATIONS, not misstatement amounts
Fraud
Profit
questions.why: Attribute = controls; variable = amounts — mixing them is the classic error: deviations don't translate to rupees without a link.

Up
Same
Zero
questions.why: More confidence = more assurance = wider margin allowance = larger samples.

questions.q: An attribute-sampling plan adjusts one factor: Tolerable deviation rate reduced from 5% to 3%. The effect on required sample size is:
o: Sample size INCREASES — tighter tolerance demands more assurance per rupee of error
Sample size decreases proportionally
The choice is not a sampling driver at all
The effect reverses if prior-year results support
questions.why: Sample size INCREASES — tighter tolerance demands more assurance per rupee of error. (Framework: size ∝ confidence and expected deviation; size inversely with tolerable deviation; population size has a minor effect once large.)
questions.trend: Core concept that appears in some avatar in most attempts under the new scheme (pattern estimate).

mem.tip: Sample size rises with: lower tolerable rate, higher expected deviation, higher confidence; falls for stratification.

questions.q: In a test of controls the auditor samples 40 items and finds 2 deviations; the reliability factor gives an upper deviation limit of (factor/40) ≈ 10.00%; tolerable rate 4%. Conclusion:
o: Test fails — compare sample rate 5.00% to materiality
Do NOT support reliance — UDL 10.00% exceeds tolerable 4%
Supports reliance because the sample rate is small
Extend the sample automatically in every case
questions.why: The decision rule is UDL vs TOLERABLE RATE: 10.00% > 4% ⇒ REDUCE RELIANCE, REVISE RISK, EXTEND, OR GO SUBSTANTIVE. Sample rate alone is never the comparison.
questions.trend: Repeated theme in recent ICAI exam question-patterns for this paper (AI pattern estimate — not a citation to a specific past paper question).

questions.q: Accounts receivable Rs 6000 lakh, planned MUS sample 50. Selection is designed how, when a few items exceed the interval (Rs 120.0 lakh)?
o: Interval Rs 120.0 lakh; big items only via random draw
Interval Rs 120.0 lakh; each of the 3 logical units ≥ interval is selected automatically; remaining dollars sampled at the interval
No interval concept — MUS is purely item-random
Interval = interval of items: 6000 ÷ 50 items
questions.why: MUS interval = Rs 6000 ÷ 50 = Rs 120.0 lakh. Logical units ≥ interval are 100% certain selections; smaller units enter via systematic interval over the residual dollars; high-value skew is why MUS shines for overstatement risk.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — the selection design is the testable half of MUS Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

mem.tip: MUS interval = book value ÷ sample size; logical units = book units whose amount ≥ interval (always selected) plus the rest via systematic interval.

questions.why: MUS interval = Rs 12000 ÷ 60 = Rs 200.0 lakh. Logical units ≥ interval are 100% certain selections; smaller units enter via systematic interval over the residual dollars; high-value skew is why MUS shines for overstatement risk.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).

questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — threshold-vs-PM confusion is the exact trap in analytics questions AI prediction, not a certainty.

questions.q: Management's related-party list carries 12 counterparties; 18 appear in the notes. SA 550 design of work:
o: Tick only disclosed transactions — that is the audit
Refuse reliance on the register and confirm with each counterparty instead
Sample any 12 — disclosures need no testing

Test the 18 disclosed first, then run completeness searches (inquiry, register cross-check, shareholder/DP data, unusual credits, bank confirmations with related-party boxes) — the gap (-6) is the real risk
questions.why: The risk in RPTs is UNDISCLOSED relationships (names hidden, structures layered) — completeness procedures (register, audit trail of counterparties common to cash cycles, confirmations that ask the relationship questions, background checks on major new counterparties) come first; disclosed items are then tested for authorisation and arm's-length substance.
questions.trend: Core concept that appears in some avatar in most attempts under the new scheme (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — the 'gap is the point' framing is how SA 550 answers score Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

mem.tip: The RPT work is about identifying completeness (searching beyond the register) and substance, not ticking the disclosed list only.
